title: 'Legal Tech Market Will Be Worth $50bn by 2027...Because of GenAI' - Gartner
author: Artificial Lawyer

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Gartner supports the cluster’s central proposition that legal departments can capture GenAI gains only by adapting organisational practices, sourcing, staffing and pay structures—not merely adopting technology. It also reinforces the cluster’s requirement for human verification. Its claims are primarily predictions and recommendations rather than evidence of realised market-wide gains.
qs: “While at first technology can promise more than it delivers, that can be as much to do with adapting to new ways of working as it is to do with flaws in the technology.”  Additional information is available to Gartner clients in the report [Predicts 2024: The Transformative Impact of Generative AI on Legal Technologies](https://www.gartner.com/document/4915231).
It is essential to check the output of GenAI.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Gartner aligns with the cluster’s core view that current GenAI should augment reviewed legal work rather than operate autonomously. It also supports the importance of organisational adaptation and anticipates changes in legal-department staffing, sourcing and billing, though these are presented mainly as predictions and it does not address apprenticeship risks directly.
qs: It is not a suitable technology at this stage to complete tasks without review.

Moreover, the portfolio of legal services needed to get work done, the ratio of in-house and outside counsel expenses, the ratio of generalists and specialist lawyers, and talent needs in-house may all require significant change to ensure GenAI platforms are successfully implemented.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: Gartner supports the cluster’s principal copilot proposition by treating current GenAI as a tool whose risks and limitations lawyers must understand and whose outputs require human review. Its predictions about operational and pay-structure changes are supplementary, but it does not substantively address whether verification consumes efficiency gains or the cluster’s confidentiality controls.
qs: It is essential to check the output of GenAI.
It is not a suitable technology at this stage to complete tasks without review.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s central proposition that GenAI should be deployed selectively within redesigned, human-led workflows. It expressly rejects unreviewed task completion, requires verification, and links successful implementation to changes in working methods, sourcing, talent and billing. Its $50 billion market forecast is predictive and qualified rather than evidence of general legal competence or realised organisational value.
qs: It is not a suitable technology at this stage to complete tasks without review.

kp.k: Gartner forecasts a $50 billion market by 2027
kp.d: Gartner's 25 April 2024 press release predicts that GenAI will accelerate global legal technology market growth to $50 billion by 2027. Artificial Lawyer compares this with a Fairfield research estimate of $25.6 billion in 2022, while questioning the forecast. These are a prediction and a separately attributed historical estimate, not demonstrated growth in the document.
qs: The global legal technology market has grown significantly in recent years and generative AI (GenAI) will accelerate this growth, meaning the market will reach $50 billion in value by 2027, according to Gartner, Inc.
In comparison, one recent estimate from Fairfield research stated that the market in 2022 was worth $25.6 billion.

kp.k: Consumer GenAI availability could expand legal technology use cases
kp.d: Gartner's Chris Audet predicts that rapid GenAI development and widespread access to ChatGPT and Google's Bard will expand legal technology use cases and support more legal-focused tools. Artificial Lawyer separately observes GenAI being incorporated into dozens of tools and renewed startup activity, including businesses built around OpenAI, but questions whether availability translates into substantially higher usage and market value.
qs: Rapid GenAI developments, and the widespread availability of consumer tools such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Bard, will quickly increase the number of established legal technology use cases, in turn creating growing market conditions for an increasing number of legal-focused tools.
there are a lot more new startups in legal tech again, many using OpenAI as the core tech upon which the wrapper is added.
Whether broad availability of LLM technology means there will be a surge in the use of legal tech tools and that the market value will rapidly rise, remains to be seen.

kp.k: Gartner expects faster adoption of legal department applications
kp.d: Gartner reports significant growth in spend management, e-billing, contract lifecycle management, legal matter management and legal document management as departments seek efficiencies. It predicts that adding GenAI will accelerate purchasing and adoption; the document provides no quantitative category-level evidence for this claim.
qs: There has been significant growth in spend management, e-billing, contract lifecycle management, legal matter management and legal document management as legal departments increasingly seek technology-led efficiencies.
Incorporating GenAI into these applications will only accelerate purchasing and adoption.

kp.k: AI tool substitution may limit net spending growth
kp.d: Artificial Lawyer questions whether firms and clients will increase total technology budgets rather than replace existing tools and features with GenAI-enabled alternatives. The commentary presents budget-neutral substitution as a possible counterweight to Gartner's growth forecast, not an observed outcome.
qs: The challenge with the statistic above is whether actual usage of legal tech tools increases super-fast and that clients and law firms are really going to pay more from their budgets?
Will they just use more tools that have genAI, but the total budget won’t go up that much, because they stop using as many tools and features that are not powered by AI?
Will law firms that spend $Xm on tech suddenly double it? That seems a bit of a stretch.

kp.k: New buyers offer uncertain routes to market expansion
kp.d: Artificial Lawyer suggests that growth might come from consumer legal services, previously slow-adopting markets or in-house teams, but treats each route as uncertain. It notes difficulties selling CLM systems and monetizing consumer products where buyers have little money, and asks whether lawyers might instead use OpenAI directly rather than dedicated legal technology tools.
qs: Or, another scenario is simply that the market widens a lot, i.e. new buyers in new market areas of the legal world.
Inhouse teams may be where things can grow, although even selling CLM systems has been tough work.
Or will the growth of tech in legal actually come from OpenAI’s suite being used directly by lawyers, i.e. not on legal tech tools per se?
As noted, consumer legal is also a big potential area of growth – but monetizing products for a market where most people don’t have much money is also hard.

kp.k: Legal leaders should evaluate automation under business pressure
kp.d: Gartner recommends that legal leaders at least consider developing technologies to meet business demands and avoid future budget pressures. Audet frames evaluation of legal department automation as a potential expectation from senior leadership as other business functions pursue automation, rather than recommending unconditional adoption.
qs: Legal leaders must at least consider the adoption of developing legal technologies to meet business demands and avoid future budgetary pressures.
As various business functions pursue automation, legal leaders may find themselves facing some tough questions from senior leadership if they haven’t evaluated its potential in the legal department

kp.k: GenAI output requires human verification before reliance
kp.d: Gartner recommends that lawyers understand GenAI's limitations and risks as well as its potential. It explicitly rejects unreviewed task completion at this stage and requires checking outputs, framing use as supervised assistance rather than autonomous substitution.
qs: It will be just as important that lawyers understand the limitations and risks of using GenAI as well as its potential.
It is essential to check the output of GenAI.
It is not a suitable technology at this stage to complete tasks without review.

kp.k: GenAI could reshape billing, sourcing and legal staffing
kp.d: Gartner predicts possible changes to legal department and pay structures, arguing that partly AI-generated documents may complicate tracking billable hours. It also anticipates potential changes in service portfolios, the balance of in-house and outside counsel expenses, generalist versus specialist lawyer composition and in-house talent needs. These are conditional implementation implications, not reported staffing or pricing outcomes.
qs: GenAI has the potential to force legal department and pay structure to adapt.
For example, it may be hard to keep track on “billable hours” when legal documents are partly AI-generated.

Moreover, the portfolio of legal services needed to get work done, the ratio of in-house and outside counsel expenses, the ratio of generalists and specialist lawyers, and talent needs in-house may all require significant change to ensure GenAI platforms are successfully implemented.

kp.k: Realizing technology benefits requires adapting ways of working
kp.d: Audet argues that GenAI could fundamentally change legal organizations, while qualifying its promise: initial underdelivery may reflect difficulties adapting working practices as much as flaws in the technology itself.
qs: New technologies can fundamentally change the way legal organizations do business, and GenAI has enormous potential to do this
While at first technology can promise more than it delivers, that can be as much to do with adapting to new ways of working as it is to do with flaws in the technology.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Gartner forecasts a $50 billion global legal-technology market by 2027, with GenAI accelerating growth.
pts.d: The market-size forecast belongs to Gartner, not Artificial Lawyer, which reports it with reservations. Chris Audet attributes the predicted expansion to rapid GenAI development and widespread consumer-tool availability increasing established legal-technology use cases and opportunities for legal-focused tools. Gartner also predicts that adding GenAI to spend management, e-billing, contract lifecycle management, matter management and document management will accelerate purchasing and adoption.

pts.k: Gartner predicts possible changes to billing, legal-department structures, sourcing and talent needs, rather than asserting that these changes have already occurred.
pts.d: Gartner says partly AI-generated documents may make billable hours harder to track. It identifies potential changes to the portfolio of legal services, the balance of in-house and outside counsel expenses, the mix of generalists and specialists, and in-house talent requirements. Audet also warns that legal leaders who have not evaluated automation may face questions from senior leadership. The source does not specify a direction or magnitude for the sourcing and staffing changes, or predict the abolition of hourly billing.

pts.k: Artificial Lawyer distinguishes observed GenAI product proliferation from uncertain growth in total spending and offers alternative market-growth scenarios.
pts.d: The article's author reports GenAI being incorporated into dozens of tools and an increase in legal-tech startups, many built on OpenAI technology. However, the author treats rapid aggregate market growth as uncertain: buyers might replace non-AI products without materially increasing budgets. Alternative possibilities include new buyers, consumer legal products, adoption in previously slow markets and greater in-house uptake. Direct use of OpenAI products by lawyers is raised as another possibility, distinct from buying dedicated legal-tech tools. These are scenarios and questions, not firm forecasts.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The forecast rests on Gartner's analyst authority and a qualitative adoption rationale; the supplied text provides no forecasting methodology or quantified causal evidence.
pts.d: The press release attributes the forecast to Gartner and quotes Chris Audet, Chief of Research in its Legal, Risk & Compliance practice. It asserts recent market and application-category growth without providing supporting figures or an adoption dataset. A linked Gartner client report is identified, but its analysis is not reproduced. Artificial Lawyer supplies a separate Fairfield Research estimate of $25.6 billion for 2022 as a comparison, not as Gartner's stated forecast baseline. The author's product-proliferation observations and budget concerns are qualitative; no systematic startup count, spending study, benchmark or case evidence is supplied for them. The organisational and billing predictions likewise have no quantified supporting evidence in the excerpt.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The market forecast targets 2027 from an April 2024 publication date; operational changes have no specific deadline and remain qualified by implementation and human review.
pts.d: Gartner's press release is dated 25 April 2024, and Artificial Lawyer's commentary is dated 26 April 2024. Audet anticipates use-case expansion 'quickly', but the text gives no intermediate growth trajectory or timetable for billing, staffing or sourcing changes. Gartner explicitly says GenAI is not suitable at that stage for tasks completed without review: its account therefore requires human verification rather than autonomous reliance. Audet also identifies adapting working practices as a factor in realising benefits. Artificial Lawyer conditions market expansion on actual usage and spending growth or market widening, and highlights procurement and consumer-monetisation obstacles.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern legal-tech vendors, corporate legal departments, outside counsel and potential new consumer buyers, with different effects for each.
pts.d: Legal-tech vendors and startups are the potential beneficiaries of expanded use cases and purchasing. Corporate legal departments are the principal buyers discussed by Gartner: their leaders face expectations to evaluate automation, while their lawyers must understand risks and verify outputs. In-house teams and outside counsel may experience changes in expense allocation, service sourcing and talent mix; the direction is unspecified. Lawyers producing partly AI-generated documents may face billing-tracking difficulties. Artificial Lawyer questions whether law firms and in-house departments will substantially increase technology budgets and identifies consumers and previously slow-adopting legal markets as possible new buyers, while stressing uncertain monetisation. Consumer uptake is discussed as a market opportunity, not demonstrated closure of the justice gap.
